Post hoc analysis from a pivotal Phase III study, not a primary RCT report.
Systematic review about industry sponsorship, not an RCT of methylphenidate.
Boys attempted puzzles on 4 days involving crossing of medication (placebo vs 0.3 mg/kg).
Randomized crossover study with 6-12-year-old subjects with DSM-IV-defined ADHD receiving either MTS or placebo transdermal system.
Two doses of methylphenidate administered in double-blind placebo-controlled fashion to children with ADD.
Double-blind, placebo-control, within-subject (crossover) design with 12 children with established diagnosis of ADD with hyperactivity.
Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial with 30 children with ADHD combined type.
Cohort study using health insurance claims, not an RCT.
Placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomized, cross-over design with 13 subjects.
Children with ADHD performed task with placebo, low, medium, and high dose of MPH.
Psychometric properties study of SNAP-IV ratings, not an RCT of methylphenidate.
Analysis article about WHO decision, not an RCT.
PRISMA-P 2015 methodological guideline, not an RCT.
Acute, randomized, placebo-controlled, crossover trial with 3 fixed doses of MPH in subset of ADHD sample.
Acute, randomized, placebo-controlled, crossover trial with three single fixed doses of MPH in 26 children with ADHD.
Development of a rating scale for adolescent psychopathology, not an RCT of methylphenidate.
Review article about developmental psychopathology, not an RCT.

Double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover evaluation with 22 children with ADHD comparing standard methylphenidate, sustained-release methylphenidate, sustained-release dextroamphetamine, and pemoline.
Randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, three-way crossover phase with children ages 6-12 diagnosed with ADHD.
Research showing methylphenidate effects but abstract does not clearly describe RCT methodology; appears observational.
Randomized single blind crossover study with 24 children with ADHD aged 18-96 months (mean 10 years) evaluating creativity with and without MPH.
Responses to methylphenidate of 118 children with ADD studied under double-blind conditions.
Within-subject, double-blind study with nine boys ages 6-9 years medicated with MPH for ADHD, administered MTS, IR MPH, and placebo.
Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover design study with ADHD children observing facial expressions before and after MPH or placebo.
Double-blind placebo-controlled design comparing 50 children with ADHD and 40 HCs, examining effect of single dose of MPH/placebo on ToM and OT levels.
Two acute randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, head-to-head studies of LDX and OROS-MPH in adolescents with ADHD.
Double-blind, parallel group study with 48 boys diagnosed with ADHD evaluating pharmacokinetics and efficacy of 1 mg/kg/day MPH in five different paradigms and placebo.
Randomized crossover design with 36 boys with ADHD and 36 age matched typical controls administered VMAT as baseline and following week of MPH(IR) or placebo.
Study 2 examined separate and combined effects of incentives and stimulant medication among 17 children with ADHD-Combined type with moderate dose of long-acting methylphenidate.
Multicenter, randomized, clinical trial with children with ADHD (n=282), ages 6-12 years, randomized to placebo, IR MPH tid, or OROS MPH qd in double-blind, 28-day trial.
Meta-analysis methodology paper, not an RCT of methylphenidate.
Historical review article, not an RCT.
Multisite, double-blind, double-dummy, 3-way crossover study of 2 active treatments (MCD and CON) and placebo in children with confirmed ADHD diagnoses.

This is an RCT (35 subjects randomly assigned) comparing methylphenidate vs placebo (lactose placebo included) in teenagers with ADHD. Measures include parent/teacher ratings of ADHD symptoms and side effects. While IQ information is not explicitly stated, the study meets other key criteria. Conservative approach warrants inclusion pending full-text review.

While this is a placebo-controlled double-blind study with methylphenidate, the population consists of adolescents with BOTH aggressive conduct disorder AND ADHD - this is a comorbid population where conduct disorder is a primary focus. The main outcome measured is aggression (Adolescent Antisocial Behavior Checklist), not ADHD symptoms. This does not meet the population criterion of children/adolescents with ADHD diagnosis.

This study examines augmentation of atomoxetine WITH methylphenidate vs atomoxetine with placebo. The comparison is atomoxetine+MPH vs atomoxetine+placebo, NOT methylphenidate vs placebo or no intervention. All participants received atomoxetine throughout. This does not meet the intervention criterion of comparing methylphenidate versus placebo/no intervention.

This study involves 57 students with ADHD treated with methylphenidate (5mg and 15mg twice daily) compared to placebo. Outcomes include behavioral ratings on School Situations Questionnaire related to task performance, which assesses ADHD-related behaviors. While randomization is not explicitly stated, the study design suggests a controlled comparison. IQ information not provided but conservative approach warrants inclusion.

This is a within-subject, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover RCT comparing Ritalin (methylphenidate) vs placebo in 25 children with ADHD (mean age 9.6 years). Participants described as 'of average intelligence' suggesting IQ > 70 for majority. Outcomes include behavior ratings, academic productivity, and side effects - meeting primary outcome criteria for ADHD symptoms and adverse events.

While this is an RCT comparing methylphenidate vs placebo in children with ADHD (ages 8.3-9.7 years), the primary outcomes are executive function measures (Cued Choice Reaction Time test with incongruent cuing), NOT ADHD symptoms or serious adverse events. The study focuses on cognitive/executive function differences rather than ADHD symptom assessment. Does not meet primary outcome criteria.

This is a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study with methylphenidate in children with ADD+H. However, the primary outcome is verbal memory and learning performance, NOT ADHD symptoms or serious adverse events. The study investigates memory mechanisms affected by methylphenidate rather than assessing ADHD symptom improvement. Does not meet primary outcome criteria.

This is NOT a primary research study or RCT. It is a commentary/critique paper discussing errors in a Cochrane systematic review. There is no original data collection, no patient population, no intervention comparison. Clearly does not meet any inclusion criteria for an RCT.

This study examines attentional lapses (mind blanking vs mind wandering) in children with ADHD and adults with subclinical ADHD. While methylphenidate effects are mentioned, the study design is unclear regarding randomization and placebo control. More importantly, the outcomes are subjective reports of mental states (mind blanking/wandering), not ADHD symptom ratings or serious adverse events. Also includes adult participants with subclinical ADHD, not meeting population criteria.
